title: Carpaccio di Manzo
subtitle: Paper-thin raw beef fillet with rocket, Parmesan, and lemon
excerpt: Carpaccio di manzo is raw beef fillet sliced or pounded paper-thin, dressed with extra-virgin olive oil, lemon juice, flaked salt, and shavings of Parmesan, with a handful of peppery rocket on top. The beef is raw but the acid of the lemon and the salt cure its surface very slightly. It is a dish of great elegance that takes about ten minutes to prepare.
sourceNotes: Carpaccio was created at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1950 by Giuseppe Cipriani, named for the Venetian painter Vittore Carpaccio. The original version used a mayonnaise and Worcestershire sauce dressing. The rocket and Parmesan version became standard in Italian restaurants internationally by the 1990s. The dish is documented in Harry's Bar: The Life and Times of the Legendary Venice Landmark (Arrigo Cipriani, 1996).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Slice and arrange the beef up to 2 hours ahead, covered with cling film in the fridge. Dress only at the last moment.

glossaryTerms.definition: Paper-thin slices of raw meat or fish, typically beef fillet, dressed with oil, lemon, and other condiments. Named for the Venetian painter Vittore Carpaccio by the creator of the dish, Giuseppe Cipriani of Harry's Bar, Venice.

content.text: requires beef fillet sliced as thin as possible, then either pounded thinner between sheets of cling film or left as-is if already paper-thin. The beef must be the best quality you can find, as it is eaten raw. Freeze the fillet for 30 minutes before slicing to firm it up, which makes thin slicing much easier without a slicer.

items.prepNote: centre cut, frozen for 30 minutes before slicing

content.text: Place {{beef-fillet}} of beef fillet in the freezer for 30 minutes until firm but not frozen solid. Using the sharpest knife you have, slice as thinly as possible across the grain, aiming for slices no thicker than 2 mm.

Place each slice between two sheets of cling film and use a rolling pin or the flat of a heavy knife to gently pound it to near-transparency. Peel from the cling film and lay on chilled serving plates, overlapping slightly.

Just before serving, drizzle {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of olive oil over the beef. Squeeze {{lemon}} lemon juice over the top. Season with {{salt-flakes}} of flaked salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper.
Pile {{rocket}} of rocket loosely on top and scatter {{parmesan}} of Parmesan shavings over. Serve immediately with bread.

items.cause: The fillet was too warm and too soft to hold its shape under the knife.
items.fix: Make sure the beef is firm from the freezer before slicing. 30 minutes at a firm-but-not-frozen state is correct. If the meat starts to warm up during slicing, return it to the freezer for 10 minutes.

items.symptom: The beef turns grey before serving
items.cause: The sliced beef was exposed to air and began to oxidise.
items.fix: Lay the slices on the plates and cover immediately with cling film if not serving straight away. Dress with lemon at the last moment, not ahead of time; the acid also affects the colour.

content.text: Carpaccio was created at Harry's Bar in Venice in 1950, when a regular customer could not eat cooked meat for health reasons and Cipriani devised a raw alternative. He named it for Vittore Carpaccio, whose use of brilliant red and white tones in his paintings reminded him of the dish. The original sauce was a mayonnaise thinned with Worcestershire sauce and lemon. The rocket-and-Parmesan version became the international standard over the following decades and is now the most common format. The word carpaccio has since been adopted for thinly sliced raw or cured fish and vegetables.
